question_en: The purpose of management's commentary in the annual report is most likely to:
option_a: illustrate the compensation structure of senior executives and directors.
option_b: explain the company's goals and risks associated with not reaching them.
option_c: provide reasonable assurance that the financial statements are fairly presented.
explanation_en: Management's commentary, also known as management's discussion and analysis (MD&A), is a section of a company's annual report. It explains current results and highlights significant events. Suggested elements of the MD&A include the company's goals, financial results, and stock performance. Most regulatory agencies require publicly traded companies to publish the MD&A. The MD&A is a summary of how the company did in the past year and provides information on its achievements and setbacks. Topics management may cover in the MD&A include how the general economy impacted results, sales performance, and profitability. The MD&A may also provide investors with updates on its competition and specific obstacles the company is facing. (Choice A) The proxy statement, not management's commentary, illustrates the compensation structure of senior executives and directors. (Choice C) The auditor's report, not the MD&A, states that the auditors, not management, provide reasonable assurance that the financial statements are fairly presented.

question_en: The notes to a company's financial statements most likely contain:
option_a: details on the company's strategic objectives.
option_b: accounting estimates used in the statements' preparation.
option_c: an evaluation of the appropriateness of the statements' presentation.
explanation_en: The notes (ie, footnotes) are an essential part of a complete set of annual financial statements. They offer explanatory calculations (ie, estimates) and detailed accounting information that analysts read to improve their comprehension of the financial statements. Since it is considered a part of the financial statements, footnote information is audited. Analysts use the footnotes to understand reporting differences (eg, FIFO versus LIFO) since US GAAP and IFRS allow companies flexibility in preparing financial statements. Using the footnotes, analysts can adjust the financials to make them comparable to other companies' statements. (Choice A) The details on a company's strategic objectives and risks are written in the management's discussion and analysis, a supplemental disclosure that is not considered part of the footnotes. (Choice C) An evaluation of the appropriateness of the statements' presentation describes the auditor's report. The auditor's report supplements a company's annual report; it is not contained in the footnotes. The auditor's report is an independent opinion regarding whether the company fairly presented its financials and abided by local accounting standards.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.01 Introduction to Financial Statement Analysis - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following least likely describes the role of financial statement analysis?
option_a: Supply information about a company's financial position to market participants
option_b: Evaluate the intrinsic value of a stock based on data from a company and the market
option_c: Develop guidance about a company's future operations based on its past performance
explanation_en: The role of financial reporting, not financial statement analysis, is to disseminate data about a company's business and financial situation to the marketplace. Companies summarize data to show how they have performed and explain the results. Accounting standards (eg, IFRS and US GAAP) set the rules for how companies record the data and produce summaries. Financial statement analysis uses these financial reports to appraise a company's past, present, and future execution of its goals and economic fitness. The role of financial statement analysis is to make investment decisions (eg, buy or sell) using these reports. Types of decisions analysts make include merger and acquisition evaluations, conclusions of creditworthiness, forecasts of future earnings, and security selections (Choices B and C).

question_en: Income statement elements most likely reflect:
option_a: values at a point in time.
option_c: inflows and outflows of cash transactions.
explanation_en: An income statement shows the results of a firm's business activity over a specific period (eg, fiscal year, quarter). It displays how much expense the firm took to produce the revenue generated during the period. (Choice A) Balance sheet elements (ie, assets, liabilities, equity), not income statement elements, are reported as a snapshot in time. (Choice C) Inflows and outflows of cash transactions are reported in the statement of cash flows, not the income statement.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.01 Introduction to Financial Statement Analysis - Answers.pdf
question_en: If a company receives a qualified audit opinion, its financial statements are most likely:
option_b: accurate and presented fairly in all material respects.
option_c: unreliable due to intentional accounting misstatements by management.
explanation_en: Regulatory agencies require that publicly traded companies have their financial statements audited by an independent accounting firm. The auditor samples transactions to determine whether there is reasonable assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatements and presented fairly. Subsequently, the auditor issues an opinion on whether the financial statements were prepared in accordance with the applicable accounting standards (eg, US GAAP, IFRS). A qualified audit opinion implies that the audit was limited in scope (eg, incomplete records) or there was an exception from the applicable accounting standards. Companies strongly prefer not to have a qualified opinion since it reflects poorly on management. Qualified audit opinions suggest that the company's financial statements are less reliable than statements with an unqualified opinion. (Choice B) If the company's financial statements are accurate and presented fairly in all material respects, the most likely audit opinion is unqualified, not qualified. (Choice C) If the company's financial statements are unreliable due to management's intentional accounting misstatements, the most likely audit opinion is adverse, not qualified.

explanation_en: Common-size income statements allow easy comparison of a company's performance over multiple periods (ie, time series analysis), or of the relative performance of two or more companies (ie, cross-sectional analysis), by showing income statement entries as a percentage rather than as an absolute number. In general, this standardization involves converting all lines to a percentage of revenue. One exception to this general rule applies to income tax expense. Analysts often refer to a company's effective tax rate, which is calculated by dividing income tax expense for the period by pretax income. The effective tax rate shows how the company is managing its tax exposure, and since it will often be different from the statutory tax rate, the effective rate is a more important metric. (Choice B) For common-size statements, bad debt expense follows the general rule that all items are converted and shown as a percentage of revenue. (Choice C) For common-size statements, interest expense follows the general rule that all items are converted and shown as a percentage of revenue.

An air services company entered into a contract with a city to build a new runway at an airport. The contract price is €100 million, and the company estimated its total project costs to be €80 million. The contract calls for construction to take place over four years, and the company does not anticipate any material changes to its costs nor any uncertainty about receiving payment. Each year's costs are listed in the following table:

```markdown
| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Costs (€ millions) | 35 | 15 | 13 | 17 | 80 |
```

```markdown
| | |
|---|---|
| Shares outstanding on Jan 1 | 2,000 |
| Shares issued on April 1 | 400 |
| Shares repurchased on Oct 1 | (500) |
| Shares outstanding on Dec 31 | 1,900 |
```

The company reports under IFRS standards. The amount of revenue that this company will recognize cumulatively at the end of Year 2 is closest to:
explanation_en: In general, an expense should be recognized in the same period in which the revenue associated with the expense was earned (ie, matching principle). Sales on credit are reported as revenue in the period they were made. If the company has a history of being unable to collect all its credit sales, then both IFRS and US GAAP require it to report a bad debt expense as an operating expense for that period. Neither IFRS nor US GAAP mandate a specific methodology that a company must employ to estimate its bad debt expense. Several methods are acceptable, such as a percentage of uncollectible accounts that is based on overall sales, overall credit sales, or delinquent credit sales. The only requirements are that: the company use the method consistently; and the method fairly reflects a reasonable assessment of the company's bad debt history. (Choice A) This is known as the direct write-off method. It violates the matching principle and neither IFRS nor US GAAP permit it to be used. (Choice C) An operating expense is deducted from gross profit to calculate earnings before interest and taxes. Deducting it from revenues to calculate gross profit will distort gross profit margins.

explanation_en: A warrant is essentially an option allowing the holder of the warrant the right to purchase shares of common stock at a predetermined price. Exercising a warrant causes the number of common shares outstanding to increase. This increase usually causes the company's earnings-per- share (EPS) to decrease, so warrants are dilutive securities. When calculating EPS, warrants are treated as having been exercised at the earlier of the beginning of the accounting period, if the warrants were then outstanding, or the date of issuance. Both IFRS and GAAP require companies to use the treasury stock method for calculating the effect of warrants on EPS. An example of XYZ's use of the treasury stock method is shown below. A key assumption underlying the treasury stock method is that the average market price of the stock is more than the exercise price, so the proceeds will purchase fewer shares than were issued from the warrants' exercise. The resulting weighted average is then used to calculate diluted EPS. An example of XYZ's use of the treasury stock method is shown below. (Choice A) $1.36 is obtained when the denominator is increased by the total number of shares issued from the warrants' exercise (1,000,000) instead of the net shares added (250,000). question_en: A company reported earnings per share (EPS) of £1.35 on net income of £2,200,000 for the most recent year. It had issued new common shares during the year, and its weighted average number of shares for the year was 1 million. At the end of the year, there were 1.5 million common shares outstanding. The company has no dilutive securities in its capital structure. The amount of preferred dividends paid last year, if any, is closest to:
explanation_en: Basic earnings per share (EPS) divides a company's net income by the number of shares of common stock outstanding. Scaling net income on a per-share basis provides a better means to compare net income across time periods. Basic EPS assumes that the company has not issued other securities, such as convertible debt, that can be converted into common stock. Dividends on all classes of stock are paid from net income but since EPS applies only to common shares, net income must be adjusted by subtracting dividends paid to preferred shareholders. Adjusting for preferred dividends accurately reflects the portion of income that is available to common shareholders. In this question, the company's preferred dividends totaled $2.5 million (500,000 shares × $5 / share), so the EPS numerator becomes $10 million − $2.5 million = $7.5 million. question_en: A construction company is hired to construct a building for a total contracted value of €10 million. The estimated cost of the building is €8 million. At the end of Year 1, the company has spent €3 million. At this time, the contract is modified to include an extension. The total contracted price is changed to €12 million and the new expected cost is €9 million. The amount of catch-up revenue that the company should immediately recognize (in € millions) is closest to:
explanation_en: Both US GAAP and IFRS require companies that have convertible securities in their capital structure (ie, complex structure) to calculate and report both basic earnings per share (EPS) and diluted EPS. Diluted EPS assumes that all convertible securities were converted to common stock at the beginning of the period. Conversion usually causes EPS to be lower due to the increased number of shares over which net income is apportioned. When diluted EPS is greater than basic EPS, the convertible securities are described as antidilutive. Both GAAP and IFRS require a company to exclude antidilutive securities from EPS calculations and report only the lower EPS figure (ie, basic EPS). Company Z has both convertible preferred and common stock, but since its diluted EPS is $0.05 greater than basic EPS, the convertible preferred stock is antidilutive. Therefore, Company Z will report only the basic EPS of $0.50 for the year. (Choice A) The convertible preferred stock is antidilutive, so Company Z will report only basic EPS. (Choice C) The convertible preferred stock is antidilutive, but GAAP and IFRS both require Company Z to report basic, not diluted, EPS.

question_en: On January 1, a company has 50 million ordinary shares outstanding. During the year, the company pays INR 20 million in preferred dividends. On October 1, the company issues 30 million new ordinary shares. If the company reports INR 100 million of net income, then the company's basic earnings per share for the year is closest to:
explanation_en: Under the accrual accounting method, revenues are generally recognized in the accounting period they are earned, and any associated gains or losses are also recognized in the same period. A seller earns the revenue by performing all its requirements under a contract. One exception to the general rule is for installment sales, in which the seller receives payments over more than one accounting period. With installments, the seller recognizes a prorated amount of the total profit from the sale each year. However, the installment sales exception applies only when the seller has a gain from the sale. If the sale is made at a loss, then the entire loss is realized immediately and recognized in the period of the sale. (Choice A) Although the company's loss may exceed $2 million if the buyer defaults on payments, the firm at this point has no reason to assume that the buyer will default. There is no uncertainty surrounding the current amount of the company's loss of $2 million; therefore, the firm must immediately realize and recognize the loss. (Choice B) The installment sales exception does not apply to sales made at a loss, and the seller cannot prorate the loss over the installment period.

question_en: An analyst reviews a company's fiscal year-end common-size income statement: There are no other operating costs. If the annual research and development expense is ¥150 billion, then the company's operating profit is closest to:
explanation_en:
Common-size income statements present each income statement account as a percentage of revenue. To find the operating profit, first find
the revenue using the amount of research and development (R&D) costs. Rearrange the common-size income statement formula to find each
year's revenue.
Operating profit margin is determined from the common-size income statement by subtracting all operating expenses from the revenue. On a
common-size income statement, revenue is expressed as 100% since all items are expressed in terms of revenue.
Here, operating expenses are COGS, marketing, R&D, and depreciation. Operating profit is equal to the product of the operating profit margin
and revenue: 0.4816 × 3,797 = ¥1,829 billion.
(Choice B) ¥1,899 billion is the result of excluding depreciation expense from operating profit margin. This overstates operating profit.
Deprecation, while a non-cash expense, is included in operating profit margin.
(Choice C) ¥1,979 billion is the result of excluding R&D from the operating growth margin; this answer overstates operating profit.

securities are dilutive; both GAAP and IFRS require companies to report basic EPS (ie, EPS without impact from conversion) and diluted EPS.

When the convertible security is debt, the numerator for the equation must be adjusted to add back the interest expense since converting the
debt means that the interest will no longer be paid. This increases the net income that is available to common shareholders. Companies receive
a tax deduction for interest paid, which effectively reduces their actual interest expense, so the interest that is added back to net income is
calculated on an after-tax basis to reflect the true cost.

question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information about a company's most recent fiscal year:

- **Net income:** $50 million
- **Weighted average common shares outstanding:** 100 million
- **Preferred shares outstanding:** 2 million (each share paid an annual dividend of $1 and is convertible into 5 common shares)

The company's diluted earnings per share (in $) is closest to:
explanation_en:
Companies with complex capital structures (ie, potentially dilutive securities) may report a diluted earnings per share (EPS) that is different
from its basic EPS. Dilutive securities (eg, convertible preferred stock, convertible debt, employee stock options) are convertible into shares of
common stock. Companies issue additional common shares upon conversion, creating more outstanding shares and thus diluting EPS. Using
the if-converted method, diluted EPS is calculated assuming that conversion occurred at the beginning of the period.
Assuming the company in this scenario converted its preferred shares to common shares at the beginning of the period, it would not have paid
preferred dividends of $2 million. Therefore, the diluted EPS numerator includes only net income. Furthermore, the company would have issued
10 million additional common shares, increasing the denominator and reducing the EPS to $0.45.
(Choice B) 0.48 is the basic EPS.
(Choice C) 0.49 results from not applying the 5-to-1 conversion ratio to each preferred share.

question_en:
An analyst gathers the following data on a company at year end:

| | |
|---|---|
| Net income | €12.25 million |
| Preferred dividends | €0.25 million |
| Exercise price | €20 |
| Weighted average common shares outstanding | 15 million |
| Employee stock options outstanding | 2 million |

If the number of stock options outstanding remained constant throughout the year and the average stock price was 25, then the company's diluted EPS (in €) is closest to:
explanation_en:
The method used to calculate diluted EPS for a company with outstanding options assumes that
the options will be converted into common shares (ie, exercised) if the average stock price is greater than the exercise price, and
the company will use all cash proceeds from the exercised options to repurchase shares at the average market price to mitigate dilution.
As such, the net share increase equals new common shares issued net of repurchases.
Since the average stock price (25) is greater than the exercise price (20), all 2 million options are assumed to be converted into common shares.
The company would have used all options proceeds (2 million × 20, or 40 million) to repurchase 1.6 million shares (40 million/25), thus increasing
net new shares by 0.4 million.

simple and complex capital structures including those with antidilutive securities

question_en: A company receives CHF 500 today from a customer for a product that it will deliver two weeks from now. The company should most appropriately recognize CHF 500 of:
explanation_en:
Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognized when it is earned, independent of when the seller receives cash. The seller earns revenue upon
delivery of goods or services to the buyer, effectively transferring ownership. The timing of delivery relative to the timing of the buyer's payment
may vary by transaction.
When the seller receives cash in advance of delivery, as is this case, the seller should initially record cash and unearned revenue (a liability
account) equal to the sales amount of 500 (Choice C). Upon subsequent delivery two weeks later, the seller should record revenue and reduce
unearned revenue since the seller has fulfilled the delivery obligation, thus earning the revenue (Choice A).
When a seller delivers on credit (ie, before receiving payment), the seller should initially record revenue and accounts receivable equal to the sales
amount at the time of delivery. Subsequently, when cash is received, the seller should record the cash receipt and reduce accounts receivable by
the amount of cash received.

question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information about a company for its fiscal year:

| Selected Financial Statement Data (CAD millions) | |
|---|---|
| Common dividends paid | 4 |
| Preferred dividends paid | 15 |
| Net income | 75 |

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding is 20 million, with 750,000 options outstanding at the beginning of the year. There are no other dilutive securities. If the options' exercise price is CAD 15 per share and the average market price of the stock is CAD 20 per share, then the company's diluted earnings per share is closest to:
explanation_en:
The treasury stock method is used to calculate diluted earnings per share (EPS) when a company has issued options. If the average stock price is greater than the exercise price, the method assumes all options are exercised, increasing the weighted average number of common shares outstanding. The method also assumes the proceeds from exercise are used to buy back the maximum number of shares possible, minimizing the dilution.

Diluted EPS = (Net income - Preferred dividends) / Adjusted weighted average shares outstanding

Adjusted weighted average shares outstanding = 20,000,000 (beginning shares) + 750,000 (shares from option exercise) - [750,000 × 15 / 20 = 562,500] (shares considered repurchased with option proceeds) = 20,187,500

Diluted EPS = (75,000,000 - 15,000,000) / 20,187,500 = CAD 2.97.

question_en: A company has agreed to build a multistory residential building for a contract sales price of $10 million, with delivery in four years. To complete the project, the company has contracted with a real estate developer, who estimates the total costs will be $5 million, although changes in construction methods may result in higher total costs. The company prepares its financial statements under US GAAP. If the company spends $1 million in costs on this project in Year 1, its reported revenue for Year 1 is closest to:
explanation_en:
Accrual accounting requires that revenue be recognized when it is earned. Revenue is earned when the seller delivers goods or furnishes
services. When a contract is completed over multiple periods (eg, airport construction), either the percentage-of-completion or the completed
contract accounting method determines when and how much revenue is recognized.
The reasonable certainty of the contract's outcome determines which method is used. Reasonable certainty identifies the probability that the
seller will be paid and the probability that the seller's estimated costs to complete the project will not change materially during construction. If one
or both criteria are not satisfied, US GAAP standards require the use of the completed contract method.
In this scenario, the company believes its costs may change during construction, so it must use the completed contract method. Under this
method, the company recognizes zero revenues, costs, profits, and losses until completion.
(Choice B) $1 million is the revenue recognized if the company reports under IFRS. Since the contract's outcome is uncertain, IFRS standards
require the use of the modified percentage-of-completion method.
(Choice C) $2 million results from using the percentage-of-completion method under US GAAP. Since the contract's outcome is uncertain, the
company cannot use the percentage-of-completion method.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.02 Analyzing Income Statements - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company has 500,000 preferred shares that pay a dividend of $4 per share and 1 million common shares that pay a dividend of $1 per share. All shares are outstanding over the current year . If net income is $10 million, then the company's basic earnings per share for the current year is closest to:
explanation_en:
A company's basic earnings per share (EPS) equals the income that is available to common shareholders divided by the weighted average
common shares outstanding during the year. Dividends on all classes of stock are paid from net income. For basic EPS, net income must be
reduced by the amount of dividends paid on preferred shares to accurately reflect the portion of earnings available to the common shareholders.
In this example, the company's preferred dividends totaled $2 million (500,000 shares × $4/share).
(Choice A) Basic EPS of $7 would be the result of incorrectly subtracting both the preferred and common dividends from net income. Only
preferred dividends are subtracted from net income to determine basic EPS since common dividends are available to common shareholders.
(Choice C) Basic EPS of $9 would be the result of subtracting only common, not preferred, dividends from net income.
